document_check.note: Broadhouse KM, Winks NJ, Summers MJ (2021) 'Fronto-temporal functional disconnection precedes hippocampal atrophy in clinically confirmed multi-domain amnestic mild cognitive impairment', EXCLI Journal 20:1458-1473. Cross-sectional structural and resting-state fMRI comparison of HC (n=24), mdaMCI (n=14) and mild AD (n=6). Authors, year and the cited finding (fronto-temporal functional decoupling separates HC from mdaMCI while hippocampal subvolumes and cortical thickness do not) all match.

cited_result: Principal result: the group difference in resting-state fronto-temporal (ROI-to-ROI) functional connectivity between HC (n=24) and clinically confirmed mdaMCI (n=14), set against the null structural contrasts for the same pair (hippocampal subvolumes; vertex-wise cortical thickness).
tool_reason: The cited result compares an imaging measure between diagnostic groups at one time point, drawn from one community sample classified after assessment, with no classifier or model built, so the JBI analytical cross-sectional checklist fits.

domains.domain: Item 1: Criteria for inclusion clearly defined
domains.rationale: The mdaMCI definition is operationalised, but the telephone-screening eligibility and exclusion criteria are only in a supplement that is not part of this document. The HC group is not defined by any threshold.

signalling.question: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
signalling.quote: Recruitment and selection of participants is described in the supplementary information (Supplementary File 1). A total of 128 potential participants underwent telephone screening and 48 met eligibility criteria.

domains.domain: Item 2: Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.rationale: The source population (community referrals and volunteers aged 65 and over), the recruitment flow (128 screened, 48 eligible, 44 analysed) and a full demographic table are all reported.

signalling.question: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
signalling.quote: Participants aged 65 years and older were recruited from the local community by referral from health care providers as well as volunteers from community-based groups for older adults.

domains.domain: Item 3: Exposure (diagnostic group) measured validly and reliably
domains.rationale: Group membership came from a full neuropsychological battery, repeated at one month for possible MCI cases and given by one experienced neuropsychologist. This lowers the false-positive MCI classification rate.

signalling.question: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: All possible mdaMCI cases underwent repeat full neuropsychological assessment 1 month later to confirm mdaMCI diagnosis. ... All assessments were carried out by the same registered Clinical Neuropsychologist with over 20 years of experience (MS).

domains.domain: Item 4: Objective, standard criteria for the condition
domains.rationale: The criteria are objective psychometric thresholds from the authors' published method and are applied at two time points. Caveats: they are not the Petersen or NIA-AA criteria, and possible-mdaMCI cases that failed confirmation were moved into the HC group rather than excluded.

signalling.question: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
signalling.quote: Criteria for mdaMCI was the presence of a subclinical impairment (>1.28SD below age-referent normative means) (Klekociuk and Summers, 2014, Summers and Saunders, 2012) on >1 test of function within a single cognitive domain (e.g. memory) with evidence of subclinical impairment across 2 or more cognitive domains at both assessments. ... possible mdaMCI participants not meeting the mdaMCI criteria at the second assessment were finally classified as healthy controls.

domains.rationale: Age is explicitly named as a confounder of brain structure and function. Other demographics are compared between groups in Table 2.

signalling.question: Were confounding factors identified?
signalling.quote: Although there was no significant difference in age between the groups, there is a significant correlation between age and brain structure and function (Reuter et al., 2012; Tsvetanov et al., 2015).

domains.domain: Item 6: Strategies to deal with confounding stated
domains.rationale: Age was entered as a covariate in the MRI analyses. Premorbid IQ differed significantly (HC > mdaMCI), education was lower in mdaMCI (13.58 vs 11.71 years, underpowered test), and neither was adjusted for. Between-group differences in head motion, a known confounder of resting-state connectivity, are not reported.

signalling.question: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
signalling.quote: Due to the potential for age to influence measure of brain structure, age was included as a covariate in the subsequent analyses of MRI measures.

signalling.question: Were imbalanced covariates other than age handled?
Was head motion compared or controlled between groups?
signalling.quote: Searched the methods and results for framewise displacement, motion scrubbing or a group comparison of motion; only subject-level denoising is reported: "Control of residual physiological and motion artefacts was performed."

domains.domain: Item 7: Outcomes measured validly and reliably
domains.rationale: The protocol is standard (3T acquisition, FreeSurfer 6.0 segmentation with visual QC, CONN pipeline with aCompCor denoising), and the analyst was blinded to group.

signalling.question: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: Processing and analysis of MRI data was undertaken by an experienced investigator (KB) who was blinded to the participant group.

domains.rationale: ANCOVA with an age covariate is appropriate. However, connectivity p-values were corrected only at seed level, a lenient FDR over a whole-brain ROI matrix with 14 mdaMCI. Power is post hoc. The cited contrast (FC separates the groups where structure does not) is a difference in significance that was never tested directly, and the analyses behind it used thresholds of different stringency. The authors concede that small numbers may drive the HC vs MCI analysis.

signalling.question: Was appropriate statistical analysis used?
signalling.quote: All functional network-based statistical analyses were carried out in CONN (Whitfield-Gabrieli and Nieto-Castanon, 2012) and all p-values were FDR seed level corrected.

signalling.question: Were the structural null results analysed with comparable stringency and adequate power?
signalling.quote: Cluster-wise correction for multiple comparisons was then run with a vertex-wise/cluster-forming threshold of p<0.0001 and adjusting for both hemispheres (Hagler et al., 2006).

signalling.question: Do the authors acknowledge sample-size limits on the HC vs mdaMCI analysis?
signalling.quote: Firstly, due to this small sample size group analysis between HC and MCI, the primary focus of this study, may be driven by larger numbers of healthy controls.

overall: Some concerns (JBI analytical cross-sectional: items 1, 6 and 8 unclear; no item rated No)
overall_rationale: Group classification is careful (confirmed twice by one neuropsychologist), MRI analysis was blinded, and age was adjusted for. Three weaknesses remain: premorbid IQ and education imbalances and head motion were not handled; connectivity correction was lenient (seed-level FDR) with only 14 mdaMCI; and the cited 'connectivity separates where structure does not' contrast rests on untested differences in significance from small groups. No review-critical item is clearly No, so the review's rule gives some concerns.

applicability.concern: Narrow MCI phenotype and small sample
applicability.rationale: The sample is only longitudinally confirmed multi-domain amnestic MCI (n=14) from one Australian community sample. Results may not generalise to single-domain or non-amnestic MCI (the authors' own limitation).
